title: Cumulative assessment: Days 1–12
orientation: Attempt these newly authored items without the lesson open, then use their explanations and writing rubrics to plan targeted revision. Earlier phase concepts remain available for review. This is a self-study assessment; there is no time-to-expertise or examination-mark guarantee.

items.prompt: The researchers ____ the site in 2019 and returned home that autumn.
items.why: The completed event belongs to the stated finished past period; past simple inspected fits.

items.prompt: Which construction straightforwardly describes a former state?
options: We would own that house, with no past frame or repeated occasions.
We used to own that house.
We use to owned that house.
items.why: Used to can describe a former state. Habitual would normally needs an appropriate past/repeated-event frame and does not freely replace used to for a simple former state.

items.prompt: Which statement about I have been reading the report is justified without added context?
options: The activity is viewed over a period connected to now; completion is not guaranteed.
The reading necessarily occurred before another past event.
The sentence cannot refer to an activity that has just stopped.
The report has necessarily been finished.
items.why: Perfect progressive highlights an activity connected to now and can cover continuing or recently stopped activity; it does not by itself guarantee completion.

items.prompt: The collection began in March and continues now: We have collected data ____ March.
items.why: Since introduces the starting point. For would introduce a duration such as six months.

items.prompt: Which context most directly supports present progressive for future reference?
options: An unsupported past narrative: We are meeting her last year.
An ungrammatical form: We meeting tomorrow.
A fixed arrangement: We are meeting the translator at ten tomorrow.
A definition: Water is boiling at100°C.
items.why: Present progressive can express an arranged future meeting. The explicit arrangement and future time expression support that reading.

items.prompt: Which if-clause uses will with a valid willingness interpretation?
options: If will you wait here, I fetch the supervisor.
If you waiting here, I will fetched the supervisor.
If you will wait here, I will fetch the supervisor.
If you will waited here, I fetch the supervisor.
items.why: Will can occur in an if-clause when willingness is intended. A blanket ban ignores this modal use.

items.prompt: The condition of the roads ____ deteriorating.
items.why: The singular head condition controls agreement; roads belongs to an of-phrase.

items.prompt: Which guidance about collective nouns is accurate?
options: British English always requires plural verbs.
American English always permits no singular verbs.
Agreement can reflect unit versus member interpretation, with regional preferences.
Every collective noun is interchangeable with a plural pronoun in any context.
items.why: Collective agreement depends on construction, interpretation and variety. Singular unit agreement is common; British plural-member agreement is also established.

items.prompt: The second route is ____ than the first.
items.why: Shorter is the ordinary comparative of short. More shorter doubles the comparative marking.

options: Hardly is the comparative of hard.
Hard and hardly are always interchangeable.
Hard can mean with effort; hardly means scarcely.
items.why: Worked hard and hardly worked express very different meanings. The -ly form is not simply an interchangeable adverb here.

items.prompt: Which statement about preposition stranding is accurate?
options: Stranding is possible only with inanimate objects.
Who did you speak to? is standard in ordinary English.
A final preposition makes every sentence ungrammatical.
To whom did you speak? is the only grammatical version.
items.why: Both stranded and pied-piped constructions occur in standard English. Choice can reflect register; formal to whom is an alternative.

items.prompt: Use a pronoun object with hand in: Please ____ before noon.
items.why: This separable particle construction normally places an unstressed pronoun between verb and particle: hand it in.

items.prompt: The phrase those two damaged boxes has which head?
items.why: Boxes is the noun head. Those and two determine its reference and quantity; damaged modifies it.

items.prompt: Use advice in its ordinary uncountable sense: The adviser gave us ____.
items.why: Some useful advice uses the ordinary uncountable sense. Three pieces of advice would count separate recommendations.

items.prompt: An unnamed visitor is introduced and then mentioned again: ____ visitor arrived; ____ visitor asked for a map.
items.why: A introduces an unidentified singular countable visitor; the subsequently identifies the same visitor.

items.prompt: The guide spoke to Lina and ____, then left.
items.why: The coordinated phrase is the complement of to; objective me fits this function in edited standard English.

items.prompt: Explain why After the survey ended, the team published its findings does not require past perfect.
items.model: After already orders the two past events, so past simple can express the sequence. Past perfect could make anteriority more explicit in an appropriate narrative.
rubric: Recognise that time conjunctions can establish order.
Do not call the given sentence ungrammatical.
alternatives: A different response is valid if it preserves the specified meaning and satisfies every stated structural constraint.

items.prompt: Discuss The team is preparing its submission and The team are discussing their individual responses in British English.
items.model: The first presents a unit preparing one submission; the second presents members and plural-member agreement, established in British English.
rubric: Account for interpretation and regional preferences.
Maintain coherent reference rather than declaring either form universally wrong.
alternatives: A different response is valid if it preserves the specified meaning and satisfies every stated structural constraint.

items.prompt: Write a 90–120-word event update. Establish a past sequence, distinguish a future schedule from an arrangement and state what will be completed by a deadline. Identify these grammatical choices.
items.model:
The exhibition team inspected the hall last Tuesday and found that two display boards needed repair. While the caretaker was checking the lighting, we measured the space near the entrance. We then revised the layout and sent it to the organiser. The exhibition opens at ten on Saturday, according to the published programme. I am meeting the designer on Friday to check the final signs. By Friday evening, we will have attached all the labels and tested the display screens. Visitors will be able to ask questions at a separate desk. We will report any remaining problems before the doors open.

Analysis: inspected/found/revised establish narrative sequence; was checking supplies background; opens gives a schedule; am meeting gives an arrangement; will have attached expresses completion by a future deadline.
rubric: Write 90–120 words of connected prose, excluding the grammatical annotation.
Include every requested construction and identify its form and meaning.
Check reference, tense, clause boundaries and meaning; this is self-review, not an external grade.
alternatives: A different response is valid if it preserves the specified meaning and satisfies every stated structural constraint.
